We'll walk through creating a cluster with eksctl, verify it with kubectl, deploy an example web application, and explain how IAM Roles for Service Accounts give pods least-privilege access to AWS resources. By the end you'll be able to create a basic cluster, deploy a service, and identify the next steps for secure networking, load balancing, monitoring, and cost control. What operational choice will you prioritize first in your environment?

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › Overview
Advanced Container Orchestration with Amazon EKS
Managed Kubernetes on AWS: architecture, cluster setup with eksctl, deployments, and AWS integrations for production workloads.
In this lesson

Understand EKS architecture, create a cluster with eksctl, deploy a containerized app with kubectl, and integrate secure AWS services like IAM Roles for Service Accounts. Learn operational best practices for node management, networking, monitoring, and cost.

Why it matters

Kubernetes brings portability and a rich ecosystem. EKS reduces control plane operations, so teams can invest effort into security, observability, and efficient workloads instead of running etcd or the API server.

Coming up

Hands-on cluster creation, manifest walkthroughs, secure IAM integration, and operational patterns for production EKS clusters.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map directly to practical skills you will use daily when operating Kubernetes on AWS. First, you will form a mental model of EKS architecture and how the managed control plane relates to the worker nodes and cloud networking. Second, you will learn how to stand up an EKS cluster using eksctl or CloudFormation, including creating a cluster configuration and understanding its key fields. Third, you will deploy containerized applications using kubectl and manifests, verify deployments, and expose services through load balancers or the AWS Load Balancer Controller. Fourth, you will integrate EKS with AWS services such as IAM Roles for Service Accounts and the VPC CNI, understanding the security and networking implications of each choice. Each objective pairs a capability with why it matters — for example, IRSA reduces credential exposure and VPC CNI ensures Pods have routable IPs in your VPC. These are practical competencies you can test in a lab: create a cluster, deploy an nginx app, secure it with IRSA, and observe networking and load balancing behavior. screens.title: Learning Objectives — Continued
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond setup and deployment, a production EKS operator needs patterns for upgrades, node lifecycle, networking, monitoring, and cost optimization. This objective set focuses on the tasks you will perform after your app is running: maintain managed node groups, plan and test cluster upgrades using non-production clusters, and choose appropriately between EC2, Spot instances, and Fargate for different workloads. You'll also learn to instrument clusters with CloudWatch Container Insights or Prometheus plus Fluent Bit for logs so you can detect resource pressure and application errors early. Finally, cost control techniques such as right-sizing requests and limits, using Fargate for sporadic workloads, or Spot for fault-tolerant services help you balance reliability and spend. Each objective pairs a concrete action with why it reduces risk or cost. When you practice, start by enabling monitoring and verifying a rolling update to ensure your upgrade strategy is safe.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › Objectives — Ops
Node Group Management

Use Managed Node Groups to simplify lifecycle operations like upgrades and scaling, and prefer automated updates where possible.

Visual hint: treat node groups as replaceable cattle rather than pets.
Monitoring & Logging

Integrate Container Insights, Prometheus, and Fluent Bit for metrics and logs. Observability is the fastest path to diagnosing scheduler or networking issues.

Cost Optimization

Key Takeaway

screens.title: EKS Architecture: Control Plane and Worker Nodes
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the EKS architecture clearly so you can reason about fault domains and responsibility. Amazon EKS provides a managed Kubernetes control plane. AWS runs the A P I server, etcd, scheduler, and controller manager across multiple Availability Zones. This managed control plane is responsible for cluster state and scheduling decisions; AWS handles its availability and upgrades. Your responsibility is the worker plane: the compute that runs Pods. Worker nodes can be EC2 instances you manage via Managed Node Groups, or AWS Fargate which runs Pods without managing instances. Pods are the smallest deployable units and typically contain one container. Kubernetes Services provide stable network identities for sets of Pods, and Deployments manage the desired number of replicas and updates. For example, a Deployment with replicas: 3 ensures three Nginx Pods run and the Deployment controller will recreate a Pod if one fails. A common misconception is that EKS removes all operational work — it does not. You still configure networking, assign IAM permissions, manage node lifecycle, and choose how Pods are exposed. A practical test: if the control plane fails, AWS will recover it, but if a node or Pod fails you must rely on node replacements or DaemonSet/Deployment reconciliation. Takeaway: trust AWS for control plane HA, but automate, monitor, and secure your worker plane.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › EKS Architecture
Definition and Roles
Amazon EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane for you across multiple Availability Zones. You run worker nodes where Pods execute, either as EC2 instances or on Fargate.
Control Plane (Managed)
API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager; AWS ensures availability and upgrades.
Worker Nodes
EC2 Managed Node Groups or Fargate run Pods; you handle node lifecycle, scaling, and instance-level IAM unless using IRSA.
Key Takeaway

EKS reduces control-plane operational burden but does not eliminate responsibilities for worker nodes, networking, and identity.

Illustrative Example
Imagine deploying an nginx Deployment with three replicas. If a node fails, the Deployment will reschedule Pods to other nodes if capacity exists or scale nodes to meet requests. If the control plane needs a patch, AWS will upgrade it and maintain API availability across AZs.
Common misconception
EKS is not a zero-ops Kubernetes. You still design networking, manage node upgrades, set resource requests and limits, and secure access to AWS resources from Pods.
Reflective question
Which piece of the worker plane will you automate first: node updates, autoscaling, or pod resource policies?

screens.title: Creating an EKS Cluster with eksctl
screens.narratorSegment: Creating an EKS cluster by hand is involved, so eksctl provides a declarative shortcut. The general process is: install eksctl and kubectl, author a cluster configuration file, and run the eksctl create cluster command. The cluster YAML contains metadata like name and region, the Kubernetes version, and managed node group definitions including instance type and scaling parameters. For example, a managedNodeGroups entry can set instanceType to t3. medium and desiredCapacity to two nodes. Running eksctl create cluster -f cluster. yaml provisions the control plane, VPC, subnets, security groups, and node groups. This step usually takes 15–20 minutes as multiple AWS resources are created. A common pitfall is forgetting to set the correct region or to provide an SSH key if you expect node access. Also be careful with Kubernetes version selection; choose a version supported by your workloads and plan upgrades. After creation, eksctl updates your kubectl context so kubectl commands target the new cluster. A practical check: run kubectl get nodes and kubectl get svc -n kube-system to confirm nodes and system services are available. Takeaway: use eksctl for predictable, repeatable cluster creation but validate region, version, and node group settings before running the command.

keyIdea.title: Declarative Cluster Creation
keyIdea.text: eksctl uses a YAML configuration to create an EKS cluster and related AWS resources in a reproducible way; validate settings before creating the cluster.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › Cluster Creation
Step-by-step
  1. Install eksctl and kubectl following platform documentation.
  2. Create a cluster YAML that defines metadata and managed node groups.
  3. Run eksctl create cluster -f cluster.yaml and wait for resources to provision.
  4. Confirm with kubectl get nodes and kubectl get svc -n kube-system.
Common mistake

Not setting the correct region or version in cluster YAML leads to failed or mislocated clusters. Validate the YAML before creation.

Example cluster.yaml
apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5
kind: ClusterConfig

metadata:
  name: my-eks-cluster
  region: us-east-1
  version: "1.28"

managedNodeGroups:
- name: ng-1
  instanceType: t3.medium
  minSize: 2
  maxSize: 3
  desiredCapacity: 2
  volumeSize: 20
  ssh:
    allow: true
    publicKeyName: my-key-pair
Run: eksctl create cluster -f cluster.yaml. The command orchestrates CloudFormation to build the control plane, VPC, subnets, security groups, and node groups. Expect 15–20 minutes in a typical account.

screens.title: Verify and Connect: kubectl Basics
screens.narratorSegment: After eksctl completes, it configures your kubectl context so you can interact with the cluster immediately. The basic verification commands are kubectl get nodes to list worker nodes and kubectl get svc -n kube-system to examine core services. kubectl get nodes shows node names, roles, status, and age which indicate whether the nodes have joined and are Ready. kubectl get svc -n kube-system lets you ensure system services like kube-dns (or CoreDNS) and metrics pipelines are available. A practical example: if kubectl get nodes shows nodes in NotReady status, check node IAM permissions, VPC networking, and node boot logs. A common misconception is trusting nodes are fully operational just because EC2 instances exist; a node may fail to join the cluster due to kubelet or networking misconfiguration. Use kubectl describe node to inspect conditions and events, and kubectl logs for kubelet-provided logs where appropriate. Finally, confirm your kubectl context with kubectl config get-contexts and switch if necessary. Takeaway: validating cluster health with kubectl early prevents chasing symptoms later during deployments. Verify and Connect: kubectl Basics means use kubectl to validate nodes and system services immediately after cluster creation to catch join and networking issues early.. In practical terms, confirming nodes, system services, and kubectl context. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › kubectl Verification
Essential commands
kubectl get nodes — lists worker nodes and Ready status.
kubectl get svc -n kube-system — checks system services like CoreDNS.
kubectl config get-contexts — shows current kubectl context.
kubectl describe node <name> — inspects node conditions and events.
Common troubleshooting step
If nodes are NotReady, verify node IAM permissions and VPC CNI logs on the node before assuming Kubernetes control plane issues.
Terminal examples
# list nodes
kubectl get nodes

# check system services
kubectl get svc -n kube-system

# describe a node for events
kubectl describe node <node-name>
Run these commands after cluster creation. They provide the most direct signals about node health and whether system controllers are running correctly.

screens.title: Deploying an Nginx Application: Deployment Manifest
screens.narratorSegment: Deployments are the standard Kubernetes controller for managing stateless application replicas. A Deployment manifest specifies apiVersion apps/v1, kind Deployment, metadata, and a spec that includes replicas, a selector, and a pod template. The template includes container specs such as image and containerPort. For example, setting replicas: 3 for an nginx image ensures three pods are scheduled; if a Pod fails, the Deployment controller creates a replacement to maintain desired state. When you apply the manifest with kubectl apply -f nginx-deployment. yaml, Kubernetes reconciles actual state to desired state. A common mistake is mismatching selector labels and template labels; if they differ, the Deployment will not manage the Pods and you won't get the expected replicas. Another practical detail is resource requests and limits — without these, scheduler decisions and node packing can be unpredictable. After applying the Deployment, verify with kubectl get deployments and kubectl get pods. Example manifests are provided visually so you can copy and adapt them. Takeaway: Deployments encode desired state and updates; always validate selectors and include resource guidance for production workloads. Deploying an Nginx Application: Deployment Manifest means a deployment declares the desired number of replicas and the pod template; kubernetes controllers reconcile actual state to match it.. In practical terms, writing and applying a deployment manifest with replicas and labels. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Desired State via Deployments
keyIdea.text: A Deployment declares the desired number of replicas and the Pod template; Kubernetes controllers reconcile actual state to match it.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › Deployment Manifest
Example manifest
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment
  labels:
    app: nginx
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
Apply with kubectl apply -f nginx-deployment.yaml and confirm with kubectl get deployments and kubectl get pods.
Notes and pitfalls
  • Ensure selector.matchLabels matches template.metadata.labels exactly or the Deployment will not manage Pods.
  • Include resource requests and limits in production to influence scheduler decisions.
  • Use rolling updates to avoid downtime during pod updates; deployments handle this automatically unless configured otherwise.
Check your understanding
If a new Pod is created but your Deployment does not manage it, what label mismatch should you inspect?

screens.title: Exposing Pods: Service types and Load Balancers
screens.narratorSegment: Kubernetes Services provide stable network identities for sets of Pods. The simplest way to expose a service externally in EKS is Service type LoadBalancer. By default this provisions an AWS Classic Load Balancer or Network Load Balancer depending on configuration. For advanced HTTP routing, you deploy the AWS Load Balancer Controller and use Kubernetes Ingress resources; the controller provisions an Application Load Balancer and configures listeners, target groups, and path-based routing. A Service of type NodePort exposes a port on each node and can be used with an externally managed load balancer or the Load Balancer Controller. A common operational choice is to use LoadBalancer for simple cases and the Load Balancer Controller with Ingress for path-based or host-based routing across multiple services. One pitfall is relying on Service type LoadBalancer for many services — that can create many separate load balancers and increase cost. The recommended pattern for multiple web services is a single ALB managed by the Load Balancer Controller and path-based Ingress rules. Example: create nginx-service with type LoadBalancer to get a quick external IP. For production with multiple apps, deploy the AWS Load Balancer Controller and define Ingress rules for path routing.

keyIdea.title: Choose the Right Expose Pattern
keyIdea.text: Use Service type LoadBalancer for quick exposure; use AWS Load Balancer Controller plus Ingress for ALB features and consolidated routing.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › Services & Load Balancers
Service manifest example (LoadBalancer)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: nginx
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80
  type: LoadBalancer
A Service of type LoadBalancer creates an AWS Load Balancer and assigns an external IP or DNS name. For ALB capabilities like path-based routing, install the AWS Load Balancer Controller and use Ingress resources instead.
Comparison
LoadBalancer
Quick external exposure; provisions a load balancer per Service by default.
ALB + Ingress
Consolidates routing for many services, supports path and host rules, and is managed by the Load Balancer Controller.
Cost note
Multiple LoadBalancer services can increase cost; prefer ALB+Ingress for many web services.

screens.title: IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)
screens.narratorSegment: IAM Roles for Service Accounts, or IRSA, is a method to grant AWS permissions to a Pod without using node-level credentials or embedding AWS keys in Secrets. The idea is to associate an IAM role with a Kubernetes Service Account; Pods that use that Service Account inherit the role via short-lived credentials issued by the AWS SDK through the service account token projected into the Pod. This gives each application the minimum permissions it needs, which follows the principle of least privilege and reduces the blast radius if a Pod is compromised. For example, a microservice that needs to write to a specific S3 bucket should have a dedicated IAM role granting PutObject on that bucket only. A common misconception is that worker node roles are sufficient — while node roles may provide broad access, granting permissions at the node level increases risk. A practical validation is to create a Service Account annotated with the IAM role ARN, deploy the Pod with that Service Account, and observe that the Pod can access the specified AWS resource while other Pods cannot. Safety note: always prefer IRSA over mounting long-lived credentials in Secrets. Takeaway: IRSA gives predictable, auditable, and least-privilege access patterns for applications running on EKS.

The idea is to associate an IAM role with a Kubernetes Service Account; Pods that use that Service Account inherit the role via short-lived credentials issued by the AWS SDK through the service account token projected into the Pod. This gives each application the minimum permissions it needs, which follows the principle of least privilege and reduces the blast radius if a Pod is compromised. For example, a microservice that needs to write to a specific S3 bucket should have a dedicated IAM role granting PutObject on that bucket only. A common misconception is that worker node roles are sufficient — while node roles may provide broad access, granting permissions at the node level increases risk. A practical validation is to create a Service Account annotated with the IAM role ARN, deploy the Pod with that Service Account, and observe that the Pod can access the specified AWS resource while other Pods cannot. Safety note: always prefer IRSA over mounting long-lived credentials in Secrets. Takeaway: IRSA gives predictable, auditable, and least-privilege access patterns for applications running on EKS.

keyIdea.title: Least-Privilege for Pods
keyIdea.text: Use IRSA to assign specific IAM roles to Service Accounts so Pods get only the permissions they require, not broad node-level credentials.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › IRSA
What IRSA does

IRSA maps a Kubernetes Service Account to an IAM role so Pods using that Service Account receive scoped AWS permissions through short-lived credentials. This removes the need to give broad node-level permissions.

Safety note
Prefer IRSA instead of granting wide permissions to the worker node role or embedding credentials in Secrets. IRSA reduces the blast radius for compromised Pods.
Concrete scenario
You have a microservice that needs to write to a single S3 bucket. Create an IAM role with PutObject on that bucket, annotate a Service Account with the role ARN, and configure the Pod to use that Service Account. Only Pods using that Service Account will assume the role and access S3.
Common misconception
Don't assume node IAM roles are the least-privilege option; they often grant broader permissions than necessary for individual applications.

screens.title: VPC CNI and Pod Networking
screens.narratorSegment: EKS uses the Amazon VPC CNI plugin to assign Pods private IP addresses from your VPC, enabling Pods to communicate with VPC resources directly. This model provides predictable routing and security group compatibility with AWS services like RDS. However, Pod IP capacity is tied to node instance types and the number of ENIs and IPv4 addresses each instance supports; choosing instance types without considering IP density can cause IP exhaustion as you scale pods. A common operational issue is misconfiguring network policies or security groups so Pods cannot reach required resources; always validate security group rules for node-to-resource and Pod-to-resource flows. If you need network isolation, combine Kubernetes NetworkPolicies with security groups and ensure the VPC CNI has the right settings for secondary IP ranges or prefix delegation. For troubleshooting, inspect CNI logs on nodes and confirm that Pods receive an IP from the VPC and that routing and DNS are functional. Takeaway: VPC CNI gives Pods first-class VPC presence but requires attention to IP management and security group configuration. content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › VPC CNI & Networking
How it works
The VPC CNI assigns Pod IP addresses from your VPC so Pods behave like first-class network endpoints. This eases communication with RDS, ElastiCache, and other VPC services because security groups and routing work as expected.
Pitfall
IP exhaustion can occur if you choose instance types without enough ENI or IP address capacity for the expected pod density.
Mitigation and checks
  • Pick instance types with adequate ENI/IP limits for pod density.
  • Use CNI configurations like prefix delegation where appropriate.
  • Inspect CNI logs and verify Pod IP assignments during scaling tests.
Reflective question
How will you validate IP capacity when planning node types for your cluster?

screens.title: Worker Node Options: EC2 Managed Node Groups vs Fargate
screens.narratorSegment: EKS supports two primary worker models: EC2 instances in managed node groups and Fargate serverless compute for Pods. Managed Node Groups run on EC2 and give you control over instance types, SSH access, and node-level daemonsets. They are suitable for workloads requiring custom AMIs, host-level agents, or specific instance networking. Fargate removes instance management: you specify a Fargate profile and Pods that match the profile run on serverless infrastructure. This reduces operational overhead and improves isolation, but it may not support all node-level integrations. A common trade-off is control versus convenience. For short-lived or unpredictable workloads, Fargate can be cost-effective and safer since you don't manage instances. For workloads that need fine-grained control, node groups are preferable. A misconception is that Fargate always reduces cost — because pricing varies, Fargate can be more expensive for continuous high-density workloads compared with optimized EC2 Spot instances. Plan based on workload profile: steady high-throughput services may favor nodes with Spot instances, while bursty tasks or isolated workloads may be better on Fargate. Takeaway: choose the compute model that balances control, cost, and operational overhead for each workload.

Managed Node Groups
You manage EC2 instance types, lifecycle, and any node-level software. Use when you need host-level access or specialized networking and daemonsets.
Optimization options: use Spot for fault-tolerant workloads and right-size instances for pod density.
Fargate
Serverless compute for Pods removes instance management and isolates workloads. Ideal for bursty tasks and simpler operational footprint but not for all node-level requirements.
Cost consideration: evaluate Fargate pricing against EC2 Spot and reserved options based on workload profile.
Practical guidance
Map each workload to a compute model: critical services with steady load may favor optimized EC2 instances; isolated microservices or occasional jobs can benefit from Fargate's simplicity.

screens.title: Operational Best Practices: Upgrades, Monitoring, and Cost
screens.narratorSegment: Running EKS in production means creating repeatable operational patterns. Start with a testing cluster to validate control plane and node upgrades, and follow a staged rollout: upgrade control plane, then test node group updates and application compatibility. Use Managed Node Groups or eksctl upgrade helpers where possible. For monitoring, integrate Container Insights or Prometheus and Grafana for metrics, and Fluent Bit for logs to CloudWatch Logs. These tools let you detect pod restarts, C P U or memory pressure, and network errors early. For cost control, set sensible resource requests and limits on Pods so the scheduler packs efficiently and you avoid oversized node replicas. Evaluate Fargate for spiky workloads and Spot instances for fault-tolerant services to save money. Common mistakes include skipping load tests before upgrades and leaving requests/limits unset which makes autoscaling and bin-packing inefficient. A simple operation checklist: test upgrades in non-prod, enable observability before production traffic, implement IRSA for access control, and run cost review after load tests. Takeaway: invest early in monitoring and upgrade workflows to reduce incidents and unexpected costs later. Upgrade checklist
  1. Test control plane and node upgrades in a staging cluster.

Use eksctl upgrade cluster to help automate parts of the process, and maintain CI pipelines that validate manifests against new Kubernetes versions.

screens.title: Hands-on: Deploy my-web-app and expose it
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through deploying a simple web application and exposing it externally. Preconditions: an existing EKS cluster and kubectl configured to point to it. First, create a Deployment manifest that runs two replicas of nginx and includes light resource requests. Second, create a Service manifest of type LoadBalancer that selects the nginx Pods. Apply both manifests with kubectl apply -f and then verify with kubectl get deployments, kubectl get pods, and kubectl get services. The nginx-service will eventually show an EXTERNAL-IP which is the DNS name of the provisioned AWS Load Balancer. It may take a few minutes for the IP or DNS name to appear. Once assigned, you can open that URL to see the Nginx welcome page. Remember to clean up resources with kubectl delete -f to avoid unnecessary charges. keyIdea.text: Deploy a Deployment and Service, confirm pods and services are running, and access the app via the Load Balancer; always clean up when finished.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › Hands-on Deploy
Deployment manifest (my-app)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-web-app-deployment
  labels:
    app: my-web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-web-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: my-web-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: my-web-app-container
        image: nginx:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "64Mi"
            cpu: "100m"
          limits:
            memory: "128Mi"
            cpu: "200m"
Service manifest (my-app-service)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-web-app-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: my-web-app
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80
  type: LoadBalancer
Apply both manifests, then run kubectl get services and wait for my-web-app-service to receive an EXTERNAL-IP. Clean up with kubectl delete -f my-app-service.yaml and kubectl delete -f my-app-deployment.yaml when finished.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build a clear mental model of Amazon EKS and why it matters when you run production Kubernetes on AWS. You'll learn what EKS manages for you, the responsibilities that remain with your team, and the common operational patterns for worker nodes, networking, and secure AWS integrations. We'll walk through creating a cluster with eksctl, verify it with kubectl, deploy an example web application, and explain how IAM Roles for Service Accounts give pods least-privilege access to AWS resources. As you listen, envision a managed control plane that AWS operates for high availability, while your workloads run on EC2 nodes or on Fargate. Notice the hands-on commands and manifests you will see later, and keep in mind the safety idea: prefer IRSA over node-wide credentials. By the end you'll be able to create a basic cluster, deploy a service, and identify the next steps for secure networking, load balancing, monitoring, and cost control. What operational choice will you prioritize first in your environment?

These objectives map directly to practical skills you will use daily when operating Kubernetes on AWS. First, you will form a mental model of EKS architecture and how the managed control plane relates to the worker nodes and cloud networking. Second, you will learn how to stand up an EKS cluster using eksctl or CloudFormation, including creating a cluster configuration and understanding its key fields. Third, you will deploy containerized applications using kubectl and manifests, verify deployments, and expose services through load balancers or the AWS Load Balancer Controller. Fourth, you will integrate EKS with AWS services such as IAM Roles for Service Accounts and the VPC CNI, understanding the security and networking implications of each choice. Each objective pairs a capability with why it matters — for example, IRSA reduces credential exposure and VPC CNI ensures Pods have routable IPs in your VPC. These are practical competencies you can test in a lab: create a cluster, deploy an nginx app, secure it with IRSA, and observe networking and load balancing behavior. Which objective will you practice first in your environment?

Beyond setup and deployment, a production EKS operator needs patterns for upgrades, node lifecycle, networking, monitoring, and cost optimization. This objective set focuses on the tasks you will perform after your app is running: maintain managed node groups, plan and test cluster upgrades using non-production clusters, and choose appropriately between EC2, Spot instances, and Fargate for different workloads. You'll also learn to instrument clusters with CloudWatch Container Insights or Prometheus plus Fluent Bit for logs so you can detect resource pressure and application errors early. Finally, cost control techniques such as right-sizing requests and limits, using Fargate for sporadic workloads, or Spot for fault-tolerant services help you balance reliability and spend. Each objective pairs a concrete action with why it reduces risk or cost. When you practice, start by enabling monitoring and verifying a rolling update to ensure your upgrade strategy is safe.

Let's define the EKS architecture clearly so you can reason about fault domains and responsibility. Amazon EKS provides a managed Kubernetes control plane. AWS runs the A P I server, etcd, scheduler, and controller manager across multiple Availability Zones. This managed control plane is responsible for cluster state and scheduling decisions; AWS handles its availability and upgrades. Your responsibility is the worker plane: the compute that runs Pods. Worker nodes can be EC2 instances you manage via Managed Node Groups, or AWS Fargate which runs Pods without managing instances. Pods are the smallest deployable units and typically contain one container. Kubernetes Services provide stable network identities for sets of Pods, and Deployments manage the desired number of replicas and updates. For example, a Deployment with replicas: 3 ensures three Nginx Pods run and the Deployment controller will recreate a Pod if one fails. A common misconception is that EKS removes all operational work — it does not. You still configure networking, assign IAM permissions, manage node lifecycle, and choose how Pods are exposed. A practical test: if the control plane fails, AWS will recover it, but if a node or Pod fails you must rely on node replacements or DaemonSet/Deployment reconciliation. Takeaway: trust AWS for control plane HA, but automate, monitor, and secure your worker plane.

Creating an EKS cluster by hand is involved, so eksctl provides a declarative shortcut. The general process is: install eksctl and kubectl, author a cluster configuration file, and run the eksctl create cluster command. The cluster YAML contains metadata like name and region, the Kubernetes version, and managed node group definitions including instance type and scaling parameters. For example, a managedNodeGroups entry can set instanceType to t3. medium and desiredCapacity to two nodes. Running eksctl create cluster -f cluster. yaml provisions the control plane, VPC, subnets, security groups, and node groups. This step usually takes 15–20 minutes as multiple AWS resources are created. A common pitfall is forgetting to set the correct region or to provide an SSH key if you expect node access. Also be careful with Kubernetes version selection; choose a version supported by your workloads and plan upgrades. After creation, eksctl updates your kubectl context so kubectl commands target the new cluster. A practical check: run kubectl get nodes and kubectl get svc -n kube-system to confirm nodes and system services are available. Takeaway: use eksctl for predictable, repeatable cluster creation but validate region, version, and node group settings before running the command.

After eksctl completes, it configures your kubectl context so you can interact with the cluster immediately. The basic verification commands are kubectl get nodes to list worker nodes and kubectl get svc -n kube-system to examine core services. kubectl get nodes shows node names, roles, status, and age which indicate whether the nodes have joined and are Ready. kubectl get svc -n kube-system lets you ensure system services like kube-dns (or CoreDNS) and metrics pipelines are available. A practical example: if kubectl get nodes shows nodes in NotReady status, check node IAM permissions, VPC networking, and node boot logs. A common misconception is trusting nodes are fully operational just because EC2 instances exist; a node may fail to join the cluster due to kubelet or networking misconfiguration. Use kubectl describe node to inspect conditions and events, and kubectl logs for kubelet-provided logs where appropriate. Finally, confirm your kubectl context with kubectl config get-contexts and switch if necessary. Takeaway: validating cluster health with kubectl early prevents chasing symptoms later during deployments. Verify and Connect: kubectl Basics means use kubectl to validate nodes and system services immediately after cluster creation to catch join and networking issues early.. In practical terms, confirming nodes, system services, and kubectl context. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Deployments are the standard Kubernetes controller for managing stateless application replicas. A Deployment manifest specifies apiVersion apps/v1, kind Deployment, metadata, and a spec that includes replicas, a selector, and a pod template. The template includes container specs such as image and containerPort. For example, setting replicas: 3 for an nginx image ensures three pods are scheduled; if a Pod fails, the Deployment controller creates a replacement to maintain desired state. When you apply the manifest with kubectl apply -f nginx-deployment. yaml, Kubernetes reconciles actual state to desired state. A common mistake is mismatching selector labels and template labels; if they differ, the Deployment will not manage the Pods and you won't get the expected replicas. Another practical detail is resource requests and limits — without these, scheduler decisions and node packing can be unpredictable. After applying the Deployment, verify with kubectl get deployments and kubectl get pods. Example manifests are provided visually so you can copy and adapt them. Takeaway: Deployments encode desired state and updates; always validate selectors and include resource guidance for production workloads. Deploying an Nginx Application: Deployment Manifest means a deployment declares the desired number of replicas and the pod template; kubernetes controllers reconcile actual state to match it.. In practical terms, writing and applying a deployment manifest with replicas and labels. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Kubernetes Services provide stable network identities for sets of Pods. The simplest way to expose a service externally in EKS is Service type LoadBalancer. By default this provisions an AWS Classic Load Balancer or Network Load Balancer depending on configuration. For advanced HTTP routing, you deploy the AWS Load Balancer Controller and use Kubernetes Ingress resources; the controller provisions an Application Load Balancer and configures listeners, target groups, and path-based routing. A Service of type NodePort exposes a port on each node and can be used with an externally managed load balancer or the Load Balancer Controller. A common operational choice is to use LoadBalancer for simple cases and the Load Balancer Controller with Ingress for path-based or host-based routing across multiple services. One pitfall is relying on Service type LoadBalancer for many services — that can create many separate load balancers and increase cost. The recommended pattern for multiple web services is a single ALB managed by the Load Balancer Controller and path-based Ingress rules. Example: create nginx-service with type LoadBalancer to get a quick external IP. For production with multiple apps, deploy the AWS Load Balancer Controller and define Ingress rules for path routing.

IAM Roles for Service Accounts, or IRSA, is a method to grant AWS permissions to a Pod without using node-level credentials or embedding AWS keys in Secrets. The idea is to associate an IAM role with a Kubernetes Service Account; Pods that use that Service Account inherit the role via short-lived credentials issued by the AWS SDK through the service account token projected into the Pod. This gives each application the minimum permissions it needs, which follows the principle of least privilege and reduces the blast radius if a Pod is compromised. For example, a microservice that needs to write to a specific S3 bucket should have a dedicated IAM role granting PutObject on that bucket only. A common misconception is that worker node roles are sufficient — while node roles may provide broad access, granting permissions at the node level increases risk. A practical validation is to create a Service Account annotated with the IAM role ARN, deploy the Pod with that Service Account, and observe that the Pod can access the specified AWS resource while other Pods cannot. Safety note: always prefer IRSA over mounting long-lived credentials in Secrets. Takeaway: IRSA gives predictable, auditable, and least-privilege access patterns for applications running on EKS.

EKS uses the Amazon VPC CNI plugin to assign Pods private IP addresses from your VPC, enabling Pods to communicate with VPC resources directly. This model provides predictable routing and security group compatibility with AWS services like RDS. However, Pod IP capacity is tied to node instance types and the number of ENIs and IPv4 addresses each instance supports; choosing instance types without considering IP density can cause IP exhaustion as you scale pods. A common operational issue is misconfiguring network policies or security groups so Pods cannot reach required resources; always validate security group rules for node-to-resource and Pod-to-resource flows. If you need network isolation, combine Kubernetes NetworkPolicies with security groups and ensure the VPC CNI has the right settings for secondary IP ranges or prefix delegation. For troubleshooting, inspect CNI logs on nodes and confirm that Pods receive an IP from the VPC and that routing and DNS are functional. Takeaway: VPC CNI gives Pods first-class VPC presence but requires attention to IP management and security group configuration. VPC CNI and Pod Networking means the vpc cni assigns pod ips from the vpc so pods can reach aws resources natively, but plan ip capacity and security groups carefully to avoid connectivity issues.. EKS supports two primary worker models: EC2 instances in managed node groups and Fargate serverless compute for Pods. Managed Node Groups run on EC2 and give you control over instance types, SSH access, and node-level daemonsets. They are suitable for workloads requiring custom AMIs, host-level agents, or specific instance networking. Fargate removes instance management: you specify a Fargate profile and Pods that match the profile run on serverless infrastructure. This reduces operational overhead and improves isolation, but it may not support all node-level integrations. A common trade-off is control versus convenience. For short-lived or unpredictable workloads, Fargate can be cost-effective and safer since you don't manage instances. For workloads that need fine-grained control, node groups are preferable. A misconception is that Fargate always reduces cost — because pricing varies, Fargate can be more expensive for continuous high-density workloads compared with optimized EC2 Spot instances. Plan based on workload profile: steady high-throughput services may favor nodes with Spot instances, while bursty tasks or isolated workloads may be better on Fargate. Takeaway: choose the compute model that balances control, cost, and operational overhead for each workload.

Running EKS in production means creating repeatable operational patterns. Start with a testing cluster to validate control plane and node upgrades, and follow a staged rollout: upgrade control plane, then test node group updates and application compatibility. Use Managed Node Groups or eksctl upgrade helpers where possible. For monitoring, integrate Container Insights or Prometheus and Grafana for metrics, and Fluent Bit for logs to CloudWatch Logs. These tools let you detect pod restarts, C P U or memory pressure, and network errors early. For cost control, set sensible resource requests and limits on Pods so the scheduler packs efficiently and you avoid oversized node replicas. Evaluate Fargate for spiky workloads and Spot instances for fault-tolerant services to save money. Common mistakes include skipping load tests before upgrades and leaving requests/limits unset which makes autoscaling and bin-packing inefficient. A simple operation checklist: test upgrades in non-prod, enable observability before production traffic, implement IRSA for access control, and run cost review after load tests. Takeaway: invest early in monitoring and upgrade workflows to reduce incidents and unexpected costs later. This hands-on activity walks you through deploying a simple web application and exposing it externally. Preconditions: an existing EKS cluster and kubectl configured to point to it. First, create a Deployment manifest that runs two replicas of nginx and includes light resource requests. Second, create a Service manifest of type LoadBalancer that selects the nginx Pods. Apply both manifests with kubectl apply -f and then verify with kubectl get deployments, kubectl get pods, and kubectl get services. The nginx-service will eventually show an EXTERNAL-IP which is the DNS name of the provisioned AWS Load Balancer. It may take a few minutes for the IP or DNS name to appear. Once assigned, you can open that URL to see the Nginx welcome page. Remember to clean up resources with kubectl delete -f to avoid unnecessary charges. A common troubleshooting step is to check kubectl describe service and kubectl describe pod to see events if the service never gets an external address. Let's summarize the core concepts to take into your day-to-day work. First, Amazon EKS runs a managed Kubernetes control plane so you don't operate the A P I server or etcd; you still manage worker nodes, networking, and application manifests. Second, eksctl provides a declarative way to create clusters using a YAML configuration, saving you the manual steps of provisioning VPCs and node groups. Third, use IRSA to give Pods least-privilege access to AWS resources instead of relying on broad node roles or embedded credentials. These ideas are practical and interdependent: declarative creation, verification with kubectl, and secure pod identity are the baseline for production readiness. Keep these in mind as you design clusters, plan upgrades, and deploy services. Which of these will change how you configure your next cluster?

In quick reference form: one, EKS manages the control plane; you manage worker nodes and cluster integrations. Two, manifests and kubectl define desired state — use Deployments and Services to declare replicas and exposure. Three, secure Pod access to AWS using IAM Roles for Service Accounts rather than node-level credentials. Keep these three guiding principles in your toolbox as you design clusters and deploy services: reduce control plane ops by using EKS, make deployments reproducible with manifests and eksctl, and minimize privileges by adopting IRSA. These practices together make your clusters more reliable, auditable, and secure. What will you apply first in your next cluster build?
